chapter_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read (How I Taught My Grandmother to Read)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 11 periods = 550 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 9h 10min

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Activating Prior Knowledge and Story Read-Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.1): word web — why learning to read and write matters
Reflect and Respond (p.1): four oral questions — grandparents, shared time, favourite experiences

time_bands.activity: Students complete the word web around the central question of why reading and writing matter, then share responses in pairs. Teacher draws out two or three ideas on the board to anchor the conversation.

Whole-class oral exchange on Reflect and Respond questions about grandparents' languages, shared activities, and favourite memories. Teacher invites three or four students to respond to each prompt and briefly connects responses to the story's setting.

Teacher reads the story aloud, with students following in their textbooks. The reading covers the full prose text (pp. 1–13), with the teacher pausing at natural paragraph breaks to let students absorb the narrative and voice of Sudha Murty's prose.

periods.teacher_notes: Krishtakka's daily dependence on the narrator for the Karmaveera serial — and her deep identification with the protagonist of Kashi Yatre — grounds student empathy before discussion begins. Students may not immediately connect illiteracy with emotional vulnerability; the word-web warm-up helps surface that connection. Any students unfamiliar with the Dassara festival context may benefit from a brief two-sentence explanation of the harvest-festival timing.
materials: Textbook pp. 1–13 (story text and Reflect and Respond prompts)
Blackboard or whiteboard for word-web display

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.2): match eight highlighted words to their meanings
Check Your Understanding (p.6–7): cause-and-effect table based on Part I of the story

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.7): written response — did the narrator expect to find Krishtakka in tears?

time_bands.activity: Students work individually to match the eight highlighted words from the opening passage (protagonist, debate, episode, community, concentration, eagerly, convincing, guided) to their given meanings. Pairs compare answers, then the class verifies together with teacher guidance.

Teacher introduces the cause-and-effect table for Part I. Working in pairs, students complete each row, drawing on the story text they have read. Teacher circulates, prompting students to locate evidence in the prose for each effect or cause rather than relying on memory alone.

Brief whole-class share-out: one pair reads their entry for each row while the class checks their own tables. Teacher highlights the row about Krishtakka's illiteracy as the root cause threading through all others.

periods.teacher_notes: The cause-and-effect structure in this task is heavier than it appears: students must distinguish between Krishtakka's structural situation (illiteracy, village setting, delayed magazines) and the emotional consequences (her tears, sense of helplessness). Encourage students to quote the text rather than paraphrase, so the evidence habit develops early. The homework question — whether the narrator expected to find her grandmother crying — asks for inference, not recall; remind students to use 'because' in their written responses.
materials: Textbook pp. 2, 6–7 (word-match passage and cause-effect table)

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.7): how might the narrator help Krishtakka fulfil her desire to learn?
Check Your Understanding (p.9–10): six true/false statements on Part II of the story

time_bands.activity: Students share their homework response (whether the narrator expected to find Krishtakka in tears) with a partner, then the class discusses the inference question about how the narrator might help Krishtakka. Teacher prompts students to consider what resources and relationship the narrator has.

Students read the six true/false statements independently and mark each true or false, then write a one-sentence justification for each answer using evidence from the text. Teacher emphasises that a correct verdict with no evidence counts only partially.

Whole-class discussion of the six verdicts. Teacher focuses the most time on the statement about Krishtakka asking neighbours for help — which is false — and on the statement about age being no bar to learning, drawing out the thematic significance of Krishtakka's quiet reply to the narrator's laughter.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently mark the statement about Krishtakka asking neighbours for help as true; the prose makes clear she chose not to, out of pride and a sense of shame — this distinction is central to her characterisation. The statement about the narrator being Krishtakka's first teacher is an important literal detail students should locate precisely in the text. The prediction question about how the narrator might help is deliberately open; accept a range of plausible responses.
materials: Textbook pp. 7, 9–10 (inference question and true/false section)

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Close Reading — Extract Analysis (Midnight Terrace Scene)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.10–11): five sub-questions on Extract 1 — terrace scene, grandmother's tears

homework.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.12): five sub-questions on Extract 2 — Krishtakka's resolution to learn

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads Extract 1 aloud (from 'When I came back to my village, I saw my grandmother in tears' to 'Her affectionate hands touched my forehead'). Students follow in their textbooks and mark any words or phrases that strike them as significant.

Students work through the five sub-questions on Extract 1 in pairs — the MCQ on what 'never seen her cry in the most difficult situations' reveals, the fill-in on why the grandmother did not reply, the extract-analysis questions on rural setting clues and tender atmosphere, and the MCQ on what is NOT emphasised. Teacher circulates and prompts students to locate specific lines as evidence before committing to an answer.

Whole-class share-out of answers. Teacher draws attention to the atmospheric detail (the open terrace, midnight, grandmother's silence) and links these to Sudha Murty's prose style — understated emotion conveyed through setting rather than direct statement.

periods.teacher_notes: Extract 1 carries significant stylistic richness: the midnight terrace is both a rural domestic space and a site of emotional revelation. Students may overlook the setting details when focused on the emotional content — prompt them to notice the physical surroundings as evidence of a traditional rural household. The homework on Extract 2 requires students to read Krishtakka's direct speech closely; ask them to bring their written responses to the next sitting.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Extended Analysis — Themes, Character, and Authorial Message

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.12–13): seven extended-answer questions — character, theme, title, effectiveness

time_bands.activity: Students share their homework responses to Extract 2 (Krishtakka's resolution speech) with a partner. Teacher takes brief class feedback on the sub-question about what 'I want to be independent' reveals about Krishtakka's character, using student language to bridge into the extended-answer task.

Teacher selects four of the seven extended-answer questions for class discussion: why Krishtakka felt embarrassed to ask for help, the significance of Kashi Yatre in both the story-within-the-story and Krishtakka's life, lessons from the gesture of touching the narrator's feet, and how effectively the story highlights education and personal independence. Students write individual responses of three to five sentences, then compare with a partner before class discussion.

Teacher closes with a whole-class reflection on the line 'For a good cause if you are determined, you can overcome any obstacle' — asking students to connect it to the broader theme of literacy as empowerment and to Sudha Murty's authorial purpose.

periods.teacher_notes: The seven extended-answer questions are analytical and evaluative, not recall-based; students at this stage benefit from being told explicitly that 'what the story shows' is different from 'what happened'. The question about the effectiveness of the story in highlighting personal independence through education is an evaluative task — model a one-sentence evaluative claim before students write. The three unanchored questions (why the narrator initially laughs, what the grandmother's desire reflects, and the thematic meaning of the quoted line) are addressed in class discussion even if not formally written.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Binomials, Prefixes, and Idioms in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.13): match eight binomials to meanings; use five in sentences
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.14): add correct prefix (un, im, dis, in, mis, extra) to ten words
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.15): match six learning idioms to meanings; use in sentences

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.14): identify five words with prefixes from the story; write sentences

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces binomials using the example 'hide and seek' from the story text. Students match the eight binomials (sink or swim, on and off, mix and match, all or nothing, part and parcel, pick and choose, sooner or later, leaps and bounds) to their meanings, using dictionaries where needed, then write five original sentences.

Teacher briefly models negative prefix formation using examples from the story (unhappy, unusual, unfortunately, irrespective, independent). Students complete the ten-word prefix table (popular, belief, important, respect, correct, continue, understand, ordinary, interesting, possible) individually, then cross-check in pairs.

Teacher introduces the idiom 'passed with flying colours' from the story's closing line. Students match the six learning-related idioms (to hit the books, to draw a blank, to learn the ropes, to rack one's brain, to learn by heart, burn the midnight oil) to their meanings, then write original sentences for each.
Quick whole-class check on two or three idiom sentences. Homework task on finding prefix-words in the story text is set.

periods.teacher_notes: Binomials, prefix formation, and learning idioms are three distinct vocabulary micro-systems; keep them clearly labelled so students do not conflate them. The idioms task explicitly connects to the story's closing moment — 'passed with flying colours' — which makes the meaning memorable and contextualised. Students who finish the binomials task quickly can be invited to find additional binomials in the story text before moving to prefixes.
materials: Textbook pp. 13–15 (binomials, prefix, and idioms sections)

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Past Perfect and Simple Past — Tense in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.16): fill five sentence pairs — simple past and past perfect tense
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.16): fill ten blanks in a paragraph using simple past and past perfect

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the two model sentences from the story on the board ('Secretly, I bought Kashi Yatre which had been published as a novel by that time' and 'I knew, then, that my student had passed with flying colours'). Class identifies the verbs, labels the tenses, and discusses why the past perfect is used — sequence of completed events before a point in the past.

Students complete the five sentence-pair fill-ins (delegates at a conference, students verifying news, Kiran and digital payments, Varun and budgeting, Raghu and a cybersecurity webinar) individually, then check with a partner. Teacher writes the correct forms for two contested items on the board.

Students complete the ten-blank paragraph (a family financial planning course) individually. Teacher circulates and notes recurring errors — particularly confusing 'had + past participle' with simple past when the sequence cue word is present — for whole-class correction.
Teacher consolidates: writes three rule-of-thumb cues on the board (by the time, after, when — and how each signals which tense gets the past perfect). Students copy these into their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in this task is using simple past for both verbs even when a clear sequence is signalled by 'by the time' or 'after'; draw students' attention to those conjunctions as tense cues. The paragraph fill-in has ten blanks of varying difficulty — items G and I (with 'already' and 'had completed') are the most diagnostic. Linking the grammar back to Sudha Murty's sentence ('which had been published as a novel by that time') helps students see the tense as purposeful, not merely technical.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for model sentences and rule cues

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Listening and Note-Taking — Digital Literacy Talk

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.17): complete five sentences with exact words from the digital literacy talk (transcript p.259)

time_bands.activity: Teacher pre-teaches three terms that appear in the transcript — digital literacy, misinformation, Digital Saksharta Abhiyan — and invites students to predict what a talk on digital literacy might cover. Students skim the five incomplete sentences on p.17 before listening begins.

Teacher reads the transcript on p.259 aloud at a measured pace, pausing briefly after each of the three main reasons (empowerment, safe internet use, digital future readiness). Students write their gap-fill answers as they listen, using one to three exact words per blank.
Teacher reads the transcript a second time. Students check and refine their answers, paying attention to exact wording — particularly for blanks requiring a phrase rather than a single word.

Whole-class verification: teacher reads each sentence stem and invites students to supply the missing words. Teacher confirms exact phrasing from the transcript and briefly discusses how the theme of digital literacy connects to the story's broader concern with literacy as empowerment.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript distinguishes between traditional literacy (reading and writing) and digital literacy; students who conflate them will struggle with the gap-fills. The blank about 'protecting personal data' is exact-wording dependent — prompt students to listen for noun phrases, not just single words. The connection between Krishtakka's experience of helplessness and the transcript's argument for digital empowerment of senior citizens is thematically rich and worth a two-sentence teacher comment at the close.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Turncoat Debate — Language Learning and the Age of Learners

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.17): turncoat solo debate — two topics, one minute each side, for and against

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the turncoat format: the speaker argues 'for' a topic for roughly one minute, then switches to argue 'against' for another minute, without contradiction being a fault — the skill is in finding valid arguments on both sides. Students review the sentence prompts on p.17 and choose their topic.

Students spend time in silence preparing notes for both sides of their chosen topic. Teacher circulates and prompts those who are stuck by asking them to think of someone who benefits from the 'for' position and someone who suffers from it.

Four to five students speak to the class, each taking both sides of their chosen topic. After each speaker, the teacher invites one peer comment — one thing the speaker did well, one argument that could be strengthened. The class votes informally on which side each speaker argued more convincingly.
Teacher briefly connects Topic 2 ('Learning can happen only when you are young') to Krishtakka's story — asking the class to name the argument Krishtakka's life makes against that proposition.

periods.teacher_notes: Topic 2 ('Learning can happen only when you are young') is directly contradicted by Krishtakka's example; students who choose this topic should be encouraged to feel that tension productively rather than treating it as a settled question. Some students may conflate the turncoat format with a personal opinion statement; make clear that arguing against one's own view is the task's core skill. Keep timing gentle — one student who runs long should not crowd out others.
materials: Timer or clock visible to students

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Letter to the Editor — Student Voices on Adult Literacy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.17–18): formal letter to the editor on student participation in adult literacy camps

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the formal letter format on the board: sender's name/designation/address, date, subject line (four to five words), salutation, three-paragraph body, complimentary close 'Yours truly'. Students label each element in their notebooks and discuss what makes a letter to the editor different from a personal letter — formal register, specific audience, public purpose.

Whole-class planning: teacher leads students through the three-paragraph structure — paragraph 1: the importance of student participation in adult literacy camps; paragraph 2: benefits for both students (skill, empathy, civic engagement) and society (reduced illiteracy, stronger communities); paragraph 3: specific ways to spread awareness and recruit volunteers. Students note two or three points per paragraph before drafting.

Students draft their letters individually, following the planned structure and maintaining a formal, clear, specific register throughout. Teacher circulates, offering brief in-margin prompts — particularly where students slip into an informal or personal register.

Peer review: students exchange letters with a partner, checking that all format elements are present, the register is formal, and the three paragraphs address the three required angles. Partners offer one written suggestion for improvement before returning the letter.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse a letter to the editor with a personal opinion essay; emphasise that this letter is addressed to a newspaper editor with the goal of persuading other readers to act. The subject line (four to five words) is commonly omitted — ensure students include it. Drafting, peer response, and any revision all happen within this sitting; no continuation of this writing task occurs outside it.
materials: Textbook pp. 17–18 (Writing Task and format guidance)

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Kinship Words Across Indian Languages — Multilingual Exploration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.21): complete kinship-terms table for five Indian languages; Kannada column seeded
Learning Beyond the Text (p.21–22): read four informational passages on NLMA, NCFE, ELP, and CCRT literacy initiatives

time_bands.activity: Teacher contextualises the task: the story opened with the word 'Avva' — the north Karnataka Kannada word for 'mother' or grandmother — as an example of how kinship terms carry cultural identity. Students examine the seeded Kannada column in their textbook table.

In small groups of four or five, students discuss and fill in kinship terms (Grandmother, Grandfather, Mother, Father, Sister, Brother) for five Indian languages they know or can pool knowledge of — drawing on their own family languages, classmates, or the 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule. Groups compare tables across the class and the teacher adds two or three examples from less-represented languages.

Students read the four 'Do you know?' informational passages on p.21–22 in pairs — NLMA and the Directorate of Adult Education, NCFE and financial literacy, the Early Literacy Project, and the CCRT's cultural literacy programmes. Each pair identifies one key fact from each passage and shares it with the class in a quick round.

Teacher closes by connecting the four literacy initiatives to the story's central question — why literacy matters — and invites students to name which form of literacy (digital, financial, cultural, foundational) Krishtakka's journey most closely represents and why.

periods.teacher_notes: The kinship-terms table is designed to surface the linguistic diversity already present in the classroom; resist the urge to supply answers quickly — the productive struggle of recalling or negotiating terms is the learning. The four informational passages on literacy initiatives are dense with proper nouns and acronyms; students reading them in pairs naturally share the cognitive load. The homework task from the summary (talking to grandparents and gifting them a book) is a meaningful extension but is not set as a formal assignment since it cannot be verified across sittings.
materials: Textbook pp. 21–22 (kinship table and 'Do you know?' passages)
Blackboard for compiling class kinship-terms table

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, theme, and authorial purpose by close-reading a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Krishtakka's illiteracy, her midnight revelation of helplessness, and her determined decision to learn the Kannada alphabet at sixty-two.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best explains why Krishtakka chose NOT to ask a neighbour to read the Karmaveera magazine to her while the narrator was away?

options.label: A
options.text: Her pride and sense of shame about being illiterate made asking for help unbearable.

options.label: B
options.text: She did not enjoy the serial as much without the narrator reading it aloud.

options.label: C
options.text: She had not yet received the magazine during the narrator's absence.

options.label: D
options.text: The neighbours were unavailable because of the Dassara festival preparations.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have confused the timing of the magazine's arrival with Krishtakka's reason for not seeking help — the magazine did arrive, but she chose not to ask.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has understood that the narrator's reading was important but has missed that the magazine arrived and Krishtakka's barrier was internal, not about enjoyment.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is importing contextual detail about Dassara without textual warrant — the prose links Dassara to the learning deadline, not to neighbourly unavailability.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, theme, and authorial purpose by close-reading a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Krishtakka's illiteracy, her midnight revelation of helplessness, and her determined decision to learn the Kannada alphabet at sixty-two.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

1. What does Krishtakka's gesture of touching the narrator's feet reveal about her understanding of the teacher–student relationship, and how does it challenge conventional social hierarchy?
2. Sudha Murty concludes the story with Krishtakka reading the title and publisher's name of the book immediately. Analyse how this specific detail functions as evidence of her achievement and as a statement of the story's broader theme.
3. How does the parallel between Krishtakka's story and the plot of Kashi Yatre — both featuring an old woman who chooses a larger good over personal comfort — deepen the story's meaning?
items.visual_stimulus: Krishtakka declared she wanted to learn the Kannada alphabet, using Saraswati Puja during Dassara as her deadline. She proved a diligent student — reading, repeating, writing, reciting — and by the festival day she met her goal. In a symbolic reversal, she touched the narrator's feet, explaining she honoured not her granddaughter but her teacher. The narrator's gift was a copy of Kashi Yatre, published as a novel; Krishtakka read the title and the publisher's name at once. 'I knew, then, that my student had passed with flying colours.'

expected_elements: Touching feet reverses elder–younger hierarchy; positions knowledge as the source of respect.
Reading title and publisher's name is concrete proof of literacy achieved, not merely claimed.
The specific detail closes the story's arc: resolution is demonstrated, not stated.
Kashi Yatre's protagonist sacrifices for others; Krishtakka sacrifices ego and comfort to learn — thematic echo.
Authorial purpose: literacy as personal dignity and intergenerational gift, not charity.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student listens for specific information and completes gap-fills accurately using a spoken informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A short talk on digital literacy — its definition, three reasons for its importance, and the NDLM scheme.
items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the digital literacy talk aloud. Listen carefully and decide whether each of the following statements is true or false. Write T or F and give one phrase from the talk to support your verdict.

(1) Digital literacy today means only the ability to read and write using digital devices.
(2) One benefit of digital literacy is that it helps people recognise misinformation and cyber threats.
(3) The Digital Saksharta Abhiyan is designed exclusively for students in secondary schools.

options.text: Digital literacy today means only the ability to read and write using digital devices.
One benefit of digital literacy is that it helps people recognise misinformation and cyber threats.
The Digital Saksharta Abhiyan is designed exclusively for students in secondary schools.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) False — the talk states that digital literacy includes accessing, creating, and sharing information using technology, not just reading and writing; (2) True — 'helps us recognise misinformation, scams, and cyber threats'; (3) False — the scheme is described as imparting IT training to 'people across the country', not solely secondary students.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student listens for specific information and completes gap-fills accurately using a spoken informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A short talk on digital literacy — its definition, three reasons for its importance, and the NDLM scheme.
items.item_stem: After listening to the digital literacy talk, write three to four sentences explaining: (a) what digital literacy means according to the speaker, and (b) which of the three reasons given for its importance you find most significant, with a reason drawn from the talk itself.

expected_elements: Definition restated accurately: accessing, creating, sharing information through technology.
Student names one of the three reasons from the talk (empowerment / safe internet / digital future).
Student gives a specific supporting detail from the talk for the chosen reason.
Student explains why that reason is most significant using a short personal rationale.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student constructs and presents reasoned arguments for and against a proposition using solo debate as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Turncoat debate on whether learning can happen only when young, or whether a new language is necessary beyond one's mother tongue.
items.item_stem: Describe a situation you know of — from the story, your family, or community life — where an adult learnt something new that transformed their daily life. In two to three minutes, narrate what changed for them and why the learning mattered.

expected_elements: Names a specific person and what they learnt (e.g. Krishtakka learning to read Kannada).
Describes a concrete change in their daily life or independence.
Explains why the learning was meaningful — not merely functional.
Delivers the account in a clear, organised sequence of two to three minutes.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student constructs and presents reasoned arguments for and against a proposition using solo debate as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Turncoat debate on whether learning can happen only when young, or whether a new language is necessary beyond one's mother tongue.
items.item_stem: In the turncoat format, argue FOR and then AGAINST the following proposition, spending roughly one minute on each side: 'Literacy in one's mother tongue is sufficient; learning other languages is unnecessary.' Draw on examples from the story or your own experience.

expected_elements: FOR side: presents at least two coherent reasons with examples or evidence.
AGAINST side: switches position convincingly and offers at least two counter-reasons.
At least one argument on either side connects to the story's themes or a specific character.
Maintains appropriate formal register and clear sentence structure throughout.
Manages the transition between sides without contradiction weakening the argument.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student produces a well-structured formal letter to an editor using functional writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A formal letter to a newspaper editor proposing expanded community reading programmes in rural public libraries.
items.item_stem: Your school is planning to publish a notice informing students about a community reading circle that will meet weekly at the local library to read aloud to elderly residents who have limited literacy. Write a notice (60–80 words) that: names the activity, states the day and venue, specifies who can participate, and gives a contact name for sign-ups.

expected_elements: Notice format observed: heading, body, date, contact name.
Activity name, day, and venue stated clearly within the word limit.
Eligibility or target participant group specified.
Formal, concise register maintained throughout.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student produces a well-structured formal letter to an editor using functional writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A formal letter to a newspaper editor proposing expanded community reading programmes in rural public libraries.
items.item_stem: Write a letter to the editor of a regional newspaper (120–150 words) arguing that public libraries in small towns and villages should extend their evening hours specifically to serve working adults who wish to improve their literacy. Use a formal register, the correct letter format (address, date, subject line, salutation, three-paragraph body, complimentary close), and at least one specific argument about the social benefit of such an initiative.

expected_elements: All format elements present: address, date, subject line, salutation, close.
Three-paragraph body: problem, specific proposal, social benefit.
At least one concrete social-benefit argument with supporting reasoning.
Formal, persuasive register sustained — no colloquial phrasing.
Word count within 120–150; subject line is four to five words.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies binomials, negative prefixes, learning idioms, and past-perfect tense using a prose text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Binomials and learning idioms from the story's vocabulary; simple past versus past perfect tense from the story's closing sentences.
items.item_stem: Match each binomial in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| sink or swim | succeed or fail without help |
| leaps and bounds | intermittently; not continuously |
| on and off | rapidly and in large amounts |
| part and parcel | an essential element of something |
| sooner or later | eventually; at some unspecified time |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: sink or swim — succeed or fail without help; leaps and bounds — rapidly and in large amounts; on and off — intermittently, not continuously; part and parcel — an essential element of something; sooner or later — eventually, at some unspecified time.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies binomials, negative prefixes, learning idioms, and past-perfect tense using a prose text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Binomials and learning idioms from the story's vocabulary; simple past versus past perfect tense from the story's closing sentences.
items.item_stem:
Rewrite each of the following sentences by changing the underlined verb forms to correctly use the simple past and past perfect tenses, so that the sequence of events is clear. Write the full corrected sentence.

(i) By the time Krishtakka (reach) the Dassara deadline, she (practise) the Kannada alphabet every morning for months.
(ii) When the narrator (return) to the village, her grandmother (already cry) for some time before she was noticed.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) By the time Krishtakka reached the Dassara deadline, she had practised the Kannada alphabet every morning for months. (ii) When the narrator returned to the village, her grandmother had already been crying for some time before she was noticed.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student explores multilingual kinship vocabulary and connects national literacy initiatives to lived experience using interdisciplinary study as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Kinship terms across five Indian languages seeded from 'Avva' in Kannada; four national literacy-mission informational passages.
items.item_stem:
The story opens with the word 'Avva', the north Karnataka Kannada term for grandmother or mother. Using your knowledge of Indian languages, complete the table below with kinship terms for three of the six family roles listed. Choose any three Indian languages other than Kannada.

Write the language name in the first column and the kinship term in the second.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Family Role | Language chosen | Term in that language |
|---|---|---|
| Grandmother | | |
| Grandfather | | |
| Mother | | |

expected_elements: Three family roles each paired with a named Indian language other than Kannada.
Terms are plausible and culturally specific to the language named.
Student can briefly explain or defend one term if questioned.
Response demonstrates awareness that kinship terms carry cultural identity.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student explores multilingual kinship vocabulary and connects national literacy initiatives to lived experience using interdisciplinary study as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Kinship terms across five Indian languages seeded from 'Avva' in Kannada; four national literacy-mission informational passages.
items.item_stem: Design a brief project plan (one paragraph of 80–100 words) for a school-based initiative that connects two of the four national literacy programmes you read about — the National Literacy Mission Authority, the National Centre for Financial Education, the Early Literacy Project, or the Centre for Cultural Resources and Training — to the story's central idea that literacy transforms lives. Name the two programmes, state what the school initiative would do, and identify one community group it would serve.

expected_elements: Two named programmes from the four in the informational passages.
A specific school initiative described — not vague; names an activity or event.
One clearly identified community group who would benefit.
Explicit connection drawn between the initiative and literacy as empowerment.
Written within 80–100 words in a clear, organised paragraph.
